(Per Hon'ble Sri Justice B. Vijaysen Reddy) The detention order passed against Mohd. Akbaruddin @ Farooqui @ Akbar, S/o. Mohd. Mohsin, dated 06.03.2020, passed by the Commissioner of Police,
Abdul Basheer vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others on 29 December, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168023320/
1 Hyderabad City, in exercise of powers conferred under Sub-Section (2) of Section 3 of the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Bootleggers, Dacoits, Drug Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders, Land Grabbers, Spurious Seed Offenders, Insecticide Offenders, Fertilizer Offenders, Food Adulteration Offenders, Fake Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Offenders, Gaming Offenders, Sexual Offenders, Explosive Substances Offenders,
Arms Offenders, Cyber Crime Offenders and White Collar or Financial Offenders Act, 1986 (Act No.1 of 1986) (for short 'the Act') and as confirmed by the State vide G.O.Rt.No.862 dated 11.05.2020 are challenged in this Writ of Habeas Corpus as being illegal, arbitrary and unconstitutional.

2. Heard Mr. Pasham Trivikram Reddy, learned counsel for the petitioner and Mr. T. Srikanth Reddy, learned Government Pleader for Home for the respondents.
3.
Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the detention order is passed without application of mind.
The activities of the detenu do not prejudicially affect public order.
The alleged offences do not fall within the ambit of public order.
The possibility of the detenu furnishing sureties and coming out on bail, and indulging in similar offences, cannot be a ground to pass detention order.

4. Per contra, the learned Government Pleader for Home submitted that the detenu has been habitually indulging in grave offences such as robbery, extortions and theft of mobile phones in the limits of Hyderabad and Cyberabad Police Commissionerates in an organized manner.
The detenu is 'Goonda' within the meaning of Section 2(g) of the Act.

The activities of the detenu created large scale fear and a feeling of insecurity among the general public, adversely affecting public order apart from disturbing the peace and tranquility in the society.

The detaining authority passed a sound and reasoned order in public interest having come to the conclusion that ordinary law would not yield results in curbing the activities of the detenu and that there is imminent possibility of the detenu indulging in similar activities.

5. In the impugned detention order, the detaining authority has referred to five criminal cases,
which form the basis of the detention order.
The same with relevant details is shown as under:
Sl . Crime No. Police Offence Date of Particulars of Bail No. and Date Station arrest 1.
Cr.No.733 Mailardevpally u/s 379 24.10.2019

However, the of 2020 detenu continues to be in judicial custody as he has not furnished sureties.

However, the detenu continues to be in judicial custody as he has not furnished sureties.

6. The detenu was granted bail in four criminal cases, out of which in three cases he was granted conditional bails.
In Cr.No.153 of 2019, the detenu admitted guilt and he was convicted and sentenced to under rigorous imprisonment for three months.
However, the detenu was not released on bail since he did not furnish sureties in all the four criminal cases.
The detaining authority strongly believed that after release of the detenu on bail, upon furnishing sureties, there is imminent possibility of the detenu indulging in similar activities.
The grant of bail is regulated under the provisions of Cr.P.C.
Every accused has a right to apply for bail and the concerned Court grants bail taking into consideration various factors.
There is a structured mechanism available under the provisions of Cr.P.C.
Having availed statutory mechanism, the detenu applied for bail and he was granted bail.

sentences.text:
In case, it is found that the bail conditions are violated,
the prosecution is duty bound to bring the same to the notice of the concerned Court and seek for cancellation of bail.

Without resorting to such steps, invoking the provisions of the preventive detention laws would amount to depriving the right to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

In a recent decision of this Court in RAPOLU MAHALAKSHMI v. STATE OF TELANGANA1 it was held as under:
"12. Every violation of criminal law does cause a rippled in the society.

entities.text: RAPOLU MAHALAKSHMI v. STATE OF TELANGANA1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: But the ripples can be calmed down by use of normal 2019 (2) ALD (Crl.) 950 (TS) Criminal Justice System.
It is only when an offence strikes the society, like a tsunami, that as a weapon of the last resort, the detaining authority is justified in invoking the powers under preventive detention laws.

13. Therefore, while invoking the magical formula of preventive detention, the detaining authority is required to firstly consider whether the offences, allegedly committed by the detenu, can be dealt with within the normal course of Criminal Justice System or not?
The detaining authority should also examine whether the release of the detenu can be prevented by opposing his bail applications or not?
If bail were granted, whether an application for cancellation of bail can be filed or not?
Whether his detention under judicial custody can be ensured or not?

It is only after assessing these circumstances, and after being satisfied that the answer of all these issues is in the negative, that the detaining authority may be justified in passing the detention order."
7.

Personal liberty of an individual is a precious human right and before such liberty is infringed, as in this case, by invoking the provisions of the preventive detention laws, it is imperative for the detaining authority to keep in mind that the same has to be done as a last resort.
Every accused has a right to be prosecuted under normal criminal law.
An accused is presumed to be innocent until he is proved guilty.

Even before trial is commenced, at the stage of grant of bail or release from jail, if detention order is passed on vague and unsubstantiated ground that there is possibility of the detenu committing similar offences, it would amount to violating the personal liberty of the detenu.

When personal liberty of an individual is to be taken away, the detaining authority has to ensure strict compliance of law, as otherwise the action of the authorities offends right to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

In SHASHI AGARWAL v. STATE OF UP2 case t was held as under:
(1998) 1 SCC 436 "Every citizen in this country has the right to have recourse to law.

entities.text: SHASHI AGARWAL v. STATE OF UP2
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: He has the right to move the court for bail when he is arrested under the ordinary law of the land.
If the State thinks that he does not deserve bail the State could oppose the grant of bail.
He cannot, however, be interdicted from moving the court for bail by clamping an order of detention.
The possibility of the court granting bail may not be sufficient.
Nor a bald statement that the person would repeat his criminal activities would be enough.

There must also be credible information or cogent reasons Abdul Basheer vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others on 29 December, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168023320/
4 apparent on the record that the detenu, if enlarged on bail, would act prejudicially to the interest of public order."

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 8. In order to invoke the provisions of the preventive detention laws, it is necessary for the detaining authority to pass order of detention only when the activities of the detenu are prejudicial to the maintenance of public order.
The five ground cases referred to above are committed against specific individuals and relate to law and order and not public order.
Law and order and public order are two different concepts.

The distinction between law and order and public order is succinctly laid in PUSHKAR MUKHERJEE v. STATE OF WEST BENGAL3, the Supreme Court held as under:
"The question to be considered in the present case is whether grounds (a), (b) and (e)
served on Subhas Chandra Bose are grounds which are relevant to "the maintenance of public order".

entities.text: PUSHKAR MUKHERJEE v. STATE OF WEST BENGAL3
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: All these grounds relate to cases of assault on solitary individuals either by knife or by using crackers and it is difficult to accept the contention of the respondent that these grounds have any relevance or proximate connection with the maintenance of public order.

In the present case we are concerned with detention under Section 3(1) of the Preventive Detention Act which permits apprehension and detention of a person likely to act in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order.
Does the expression "public order" take in every kind of infraction of order or only some categories thereof.
It is manifest that every act of assault or injury to specific persons does not lead to public disorder.
When two people quarrel and fight and assault each other inside a house (1969) 1 SCC 10 or in a street, it may be said that there is disorder but not public disorder.

Such cases are dealt with under the powers vested in the executive authorities under the provisions of ordinary criminal law but the culprits cannot be detained on the ground that they were disturbing public order.
The contravention of any law always affects order but before it can be said to affect public order, it must affect the community or the public at large.

In this connection we must draw a line of demarcation between serious and aggravated forms of disorder which directly affect the community or injure the public interest and the relatively minor breaches of peace of a purely local significance which primarily injure specific individuals and only in a secondary sense public interest.

A mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is thus not necessarily sufficient for action under the Preventive Detention Act but a disturbance which will affect public order comes within the scope of the Act."
"The difference between the concepts of 'public order' and law and order' is similar to the distinction between 'public' and 'private' crimes in the realm of jurisprudence.

In considering the material elements of crime, the historic tests which each community applies are intrinsic wrongfulness and social expediency which are the two most important factors which have led to the designation of certain conduct as criminal.

Dr. Allen has distinguished 'public' and 'private' crimes in the sense that some offences primarily injure specific persons and only secondarily the public interest,
while others directly injure the public interest 'and affect individuals only remotely.

Abdul Basheer vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others on 29 December, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168023320/
5

entities.text: Abdul Basheer vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: (See Dr. Allen's Legal Duties, p.249).

There is a broad distinction along these lines,
but differences naturally arise in the application of any such test.

The learned author has pointed out that out of 331 indictable English offences 203 are public wrongs and 128 private wrongs."
9.
An order of detention has to be resorted as an extreme and last step only when attempts made by the authorities to deal with and prosecute the detenu under ordinary law do not yield results.

The preventive detention laws cannot be invoked as an easy way method bypassing the ordinary law and if detention order is passed, it is very much necessary for the detaining authority to apply its mind and arrive at a conclusion that ordinary law is not capable of acting deterrent against the detenu and thus, detention order needs to be passed.

The High Court of Judicature for the State of Telangana and the State of Andhra Pradesh in C. NEELA v. STATE OF TELANGNA4 held as under:
"...The State cannot find an easy way out by choosing to invoke the draconian provisions of preventive detention laws against every criminal as a substitute for his prosecution.

entities.text: High Court of Judicature for the State of Telangana
entities.label: COURT

entities.text: C. NEELA v. STATE OF TELANGNA4
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
As discussed supra, the Supreme Court has drawn a clear distinction between disturbance to public order on one side and disturbance to law and order on the other and held that only in the former case the State is permitted to invoke the powers under the preventive detention laws."
10.
In view of the above, this Court finds that the impugned detention order is unsustainable and liable to be set aside and accordingly set aside.
The writ petition is allowed.
The impugned detention order dated 06.03.2020 and the confirmation order dated 11.05.2020 are hereby set aside.

The respondents are directed to set the detenu, namely Mohd. Akbaruddin Farooqui @ Akbar, S/o. Mohd. Mohsin, at liberty forthwith, in case he is no longer detained in the criminal cases which have been registered so far against him.
As a sequel, the miscellaneous petitions, pending if any, shall stand closed.
There shall be no order as to costs.
RAGHVENDRA SINGH CHAUHAN, CJ __________________ B. VIJAYSEN REDDY, J December 29, 2020 DSK 2017 (2) ALD (Crl.)
